content:
The [Unix Time Converter](/unix-time-converter) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Convert Unix timestamps to dates and back — plus the current time. Enter your convert, unix timestamp (seconds) and date (e.g. 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Convert between Unix timestamps — the number of seconds since 1 January 1970 (UTC) — and human-readable dates. Programmers meet timestamps everywhere: in APIs, databases, log files and JWTs. Paste a timestamp to see the date, paste a date to get the timestamp, or read the current Unix time. A 13-digit value is treated as milliseconds, which is what JavaScript's Date.now() returns. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Unix Time Converter

Start by choosing your convert from the list, then typing or pasting your unix timestamp (seconds) and finally typing or pasting your date (e.g. 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Choose the direction: timestamp to date, date to timestamp, or the current time.
2. Enter the timestamp (seconds — a 13-digit value is read as milliseconds) or the date.
3. Read the converted value in UTC.

## Formula

Unix timestamp = seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Date = 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z + timestamp seconds. For example, 1700000000 is 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Unix Time Converter](/unix-time-converter) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. The timestamp 1700000000 is Tuesday, November 14, 2023 at 10:13:20 PM UTC. The same date in milliseconds is 1700000000000. Try the same figures in the [Unix Time Converter](/unix-time-converter) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Convert: Unix timestamp → date, Unix timestamp (seconds): 1700000000, Date (e.g. 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z): 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z), the [Unix Time Converter](/unix-time-converter) returns UTC date: 2023-11-14T22:13:20.000Z, Readable (UTC): Tuesday, November 14, 2023 at 10:13:20 PM UTC, Unix timestamp: 1700000000, Milliseconds: 1700000000000. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Age Calculator](/age-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Seconds or milliseconds?

Unix time is traditionally seconds — 1700000000 is 10 digits. JavaScript's Date.now() returns milliseconds — 1700000000000, 13 digits. Mixing them up is one of the most common bugs in programming: a milliseconds value read as seconds points to the year 55,000. This converter detects 13-digit values and treats them as milliseconds automatically.

## Why 1970?

Unix time counts from 1 January 1970, the “epoch” chosen when Unix was built. It is the same everywhere in the world — a timestamp means the same instant in every time zone, which is why servers store it and only convert to local time for display. The 32-bit version of Unix time runs out in 2038, but modern systems use 64-bit timestamps, which last effectively forever.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- 13-digit values are milliseconds — the converter handles both.
- Timestamps are always UTC; convert to local time only for display.
- The “current time” mode updates every time the page loads.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is Unix time?

The number of seconds since 1 January 1970, 00:00:00 UTC. It is the standard way computers store a moment in time, because it means the same instant in every time zone. Try it with your own numbers in the [Unix Time Converter](/unix-time-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the current Unix timestamp?

Use the “Current Unix time” mode — it reads the clock and shows the timestamp in seconds and milliseconds, plus the UTC date. Try it with your own numbers in the [Unix Time Converter](/unix-time-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why does my timestamp show the year 55,000?

You have a milliseconds value (13 digits) being read as seconds. Divide by 1,000, or paste it here — this converter detects 13-digit values automatically. Try it with your own numbers in the [Unix Time Converter](/unix-time-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Is Unix time the same in every time zone?

Yes. A timestamp is one instant; only the display changes with the time zone. 1700000000 is 22:13 UTC and 17:13 in New York on the same day. Try it with your own numbers in the [Unix Time Converter](/unix-time-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
